Section 10.1 — The Christian in the World: Citizenship, Culture, and Discernment

The believer lives in two kingdoms at once, and learning to do so faithfully is no small part of Christian ethics. Our Lord settled the basic principle when He held up a coin and said, "Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's" (Matthew 22:21). The Christian owes the governing authorities real obedience — Paul tells us they are ordained of God and we are to be subject to them (Romans 13:1) — and yet that obedience is never absolute, for Caesar himself belongs to God, and when the state commands what God forbids or forbids what God commands, we must obey God rather than men. The pastor must teach his people to be the best of citizens and never the state's lapdogs, honoring the magistrate without ever handing him the conscience that belongs to God alone.

The same wisdom governs the believer's stance toward the wider culture, and here two opposite errors beckon. One is the fortress — withdrawal into a Christian bunker, refusing all engagement, hiding the light under a basket. The other is the chameleon — blending so completely into the surrounding culture that the church becomes indistinguishable from the world it was meant to transform. Scripture rejects both: "do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind" (Romans 12:2). We are neither to flee the world nor to be squeezed into its mold, but to engage it with discernment — and that discernment extends to the screens, the media, and the technologies that now disciple our people more hours of the week than we do. Teach your flock to weigh what they watch and consume, neither swallowing the culture whole nor fearing it, but testing all things and holding fast what is good.

One further sphere belongs here: the care of God's creation. The dominion granted to humanity in the beginning was never a license to plunder but a charge to steward; Adam was placed in the garden "to tend and keep it" (Genesis 2:15). The Christian neither worships the creation as the pagan does nor despises it as the careless do, but cares for it as a faithful steward of what belongs to God — one more arena in which our ethics confess whose world this is.
Section 10.2 — Judged for Judging: Discernment Without Hypocrisy

No verse is more often hurled at the faithful pastor than our Lord's "Judge not, that you be not judged" (Matthew 7:1), wielded by a culture that means by it that no one may ever call anything wrong. So we must understand the passage rightly, because a misreading disarms the church and a right reading arms her. Jesus is not forbidding all moral discernment — that would contradict His own commands and the rest of Scripture. He is forbidding hypocritical judgment, the judgment of a man with a plank in his own eye fussing over the speck in his brother's. And notice what He commands after the rebuke: "First remove the plank from your own eye, and then you will see clearly to remove the speck from your brother's eye" (Matthew 7:5). The goal is not to stop helping the brother; it is to deal with yourself first so that you can help him without hypocrisy. Self-examination comes first — always first — and that order must be at least as sharp in the pastor's heart as his readiness to correct others, or he becomes the very hypocrite the Lord condemns.

Once the plank is out, however, the church is not only permitted but commanded to judge. Our Lord said elsewhere, "Do not judge according to appearance, but judge with righteous judgment" (John 7:24) — not do not judge, but judge rightly. Paul rebuked the Corinthians for failing to judge a sinning member, saying plainly that while we do not judge outsiders, "do you not judge those who are inside?" (1 Corinthians 5:12). The discernment that distinguishes good from evil, names sin as sin, and lovingly corrects the erring brother is not the forbidden thing; it is Christian maturity, the very thing Hebrews said the mature possess. What is forbidden is the censorious, hypocritical, self-righteous spirit that condemns others to feel superior.

So the faithful pastor needs courage — courage to teach the truth and call sin by its name in an age that will brand him "judgmental" for doing so. But that courage must be wedded, every step, to the humility of a man who has first judged himself. Discernment without self-examination curdles into Pharisaism; self-examination without discernment collapses into cowardice. The shepherd is called to both at once.
Section 10.3 — Restoring the Fallen: The Goal of All Discipline

We said in Unit 6 that the first purpose of all church discipline is the restoration of the sinner, never his destruction. Now we must learn how that restoration is actually accomplished, for it is one of the most delicate and most neglected works of the ministry. The pattern is given in 2 Corinthians 2, where Paul writes about a repentant offender under discipline — traditionally identified with the man of 1 Corinthians 5, though scholars debate whether this is the same case or a separate offense from Paul's painful visit; the pastoral principle holds either way. The man has now repented — and Paul's instruction is urgent and tender. The punishment has done its work; therefore, he says, the church must do three things: "you ought rather to forgive and comfort him, lest perhaps such a one be swallowed up with too much sorrow" (2 Corinthians 2:7), and then, "reaffirm your love to him" (2:8). Forgive, comfort, reaffirm love. Discipline that does not aim relentlessly at this glad ending has missed its purpose entirely.

Two warnings frame the process. Paul says to restore the penitent "lest Satan should take advantage of us" (2 Corinthians 2:11) — for the enemy is as pleased by a church that will not forgive the repentant as by the sin that began it all. The danger runs in both directions. But genuine restoration also requires the discernment we have just studied: the pastor must distinguish true repentance from its counterfeit, "godly sorrow" that "produces repentance leading to salvation" from the merely "sorrow of the world" that is only regret at being caught (2 Corinthians 7:10). Real repentance bears fruit; it is not mere tears but a turning.

From this flow the practical wisdom of restoration: a process that is neither rushed nor refused. To restore a fallen man too quickly — especially a fallen leader — before repentance has been tested and trust rebuilt, is to wound the church and often the man himself; but to refuse ever to restore a truly penitent brother is the unforgiving cruelty Paul expressly forbids. Wise restoration often takes the form of a clear, written path: defined steps, a season of proven faithfulness, gradual reintegration into fellowship and, where appropriate and only in time, into service, with ongoing care long after the formal process has ended. The aim throughout is a brother fully healed and a body made whole, to the glory of the God who restores.
Cross-Reference · Unit 6This section completes the treatment of church discipline begun in Section 6.3, where restoration was named as discipline’s first and unbending goal.
Section 10.4 — Capstone: Living and Finishing Faithfully

We come to the end of our course, and it is fitting to gather what we have learned into a life rather than leave it as a list. Across ten units we have seen one truth hold everything together: Christian ethics is never a ladder we climb to earn God's favor, but the fruit of a favor already given. We began there in Unit 1, and we have refused all the way through to reverse it. Grace first, always first — and then the holy life that grace produces. Every duty we have studied, from the guarding of the marriage bed to the handling of the church's money to the restoration of the fallen, is simply what gratitude looks like when it is worked out in the thousand decisions of a ministry.

To help you carry it, I urge you to do what faithful ministers have long done: write your own Pastoral Ethics Statement — a settled, personal declaration of the convictions and commitments by which you will conduct your ministry, drawn from all we have covered. Decide in the calm, as we said of the ministerial code in Unit 5, what you will do in the storm. Commit it to paper, submit it to accountability, and review it on your knees. And resolve upon a lifetime of vigilance, for as we learned in Unit 3, no man falls all at once; he drifts, and only watchfulness and honest brothers keep a man from the slow slide.

Let me leave you with the sobering picture our Lord Himself used, the rich man and Lazarus (Luke 16). A wealthy man feasted in comfort every day while a beggar named Lazarus lay at his gate, longing for the crumbs. The rich man did Lazarus no violence; his sin was simply that he stepped over him, day after day, and did nothing. Then both men died, and the comfortable man "in torments... lifted up his eyes" and saw, too late, across an unbridgeable gulf, the beggar he had ignored now comforted in glory. There is the great reversal that ought to govern how a pastor lives, gives, judges, and shepherds now — for we will all lift up our eyes one day and give account. Do not be the man who steps over the Lazarus at his gate, whether that Lazarus is the poor, the fallen brother awaiting restoration, the wounded soul in the pew, or the family in his own home. See the person God has set before you. Spend yourself for him.

And so we end where a faithful ministry ends, with the testimony first sounded in Unit 3: "I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith" (2 Timothy 4:7). The goal was never merely to begin well, nor to be admired, nor to avoid scandal. The goal is to finish — to stand at the last having been, by the grace of God, a faithful and holy shepherd of the flock He bought with His own blood. May God grant it to every man who has studied these things, and may the grace that called you keep you to the end.

Cross-Reference · The Whole CourseThis capstone gathers the threads of all ten units: the grace-before-works order (Units 1–2), the slow-drift vigilance (Unit 3), the ministerial code (Unit 5), the restoration goal (Unit 6), the image of God in every person (Unit 7), and the call to see and serve the poor (Unit 9).

sa.prompt: 21. Explain the two-kingdoms principle and the limit on obedience to the state.
sa.model: Jesus settled the basic principle by saying, render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's. The Christian's obedience to governing authorities is real, yet never absolute. When the state commands what God forbids, the believer must obey God rather than men. The two kingdoms each have their claim, but God's is supreme where they conflict.

es_reference.prompt: 21. Explique el principio de los dos reinos y el límite de la obediencia al estado.
es_reference.model: Jesús sentó el principio básico al decir: dad a César lo que es de César, y a Dios lo que es de Dios. La obediencia del cristiano a las autoridades que gobiernan es real, pero nunca absoluta. Cuando el estado manda lo que Dios prohíbe, el creyente debe obedecer a Dios antes que a los hombres. Los dos reinos tienen cada uno su reclamo, pero el de Dios es supremo donde entran en conflicto.

sa.prompt: 22. Describe the fortress and the chameleon as opposite errors in engaging culture.
sa.model: In engaging culture the believer can fall into two opposite errors. The fortress withdraws entirely, sealing itself off from the world; the chameleon absorbs the world's color until it is indistinguishable from it. Romans 12:2 charts the path between: be not conformed to this world, but transformed by the renewing of the mind. The Christian neither flees the culture nor dissolves into it, but engages it with a renewed mind.

es_reference.prompt: 22. Describa la fortaleza y el camaleón como errores opuestos al relacionarse con la cultura.
es_reference.model: Al relacionarse con la cultura el creyente puede caer en dos errores opuestos. La fortaleza se retira por completo, aislándose del mundo; el camaleón absorbe el color del mundo hasta volverse indistinguible de él. Romanos 12:2 traza el camino intermedio: no os conforméis a este mundo, mas transformaos por la renovación de vuestro entendimiento. El cristiano ni huye de la cultura ni se disuelve en ella, sino que la enfrenta con una mente renovada.

sa.prompt: 23. Explain 'Judge not' rightly, distinguishing forbidden judgment from required discernment.
sa.model: 'Judge not, that you be not judged' (Matthew 7:1) forbids hypocritical, self-righteous judgment, not all moral discernment. Jesus tells the hearer first to remove the plank from his own eye—and then he can see clearly to help his brother; John 7:24 commands judging with righteous judgment, and 1 Corinthians 5:12 says the church judges those inside. Discernment without self-examination curdles into Pharisaism, while self-examination without discernment collapses into cowardice. The pastor needs courage to name sin in an age that will brand him judgmental.

es_reference.prompt: 23. Explique correctamente «No juzguéis», distinguiendo el juicio prohibido del discernimiento requerido.
es_reference.model: «No juzguéis, para que no seáis juzgados» (Mateo 7:1) prohíbe el juicio hipócrita y farisaico, no todo discernimiento moral. Jesús manda al oyente sacar primero la viga de su propio ojo — y entonces verá claramente para ayudar a su hermano; Juan 7:24 ordena juzgar con justo juicio, y 1 Corintios 5:12 dice que la iglesia juzga a los que están dentro. El discernimiento sin examen propio se cuaja en fariseísmo, mientras que el examen propio sin discernimiento se desploma en cobardía. El pastor necesita valor para llamar al pecado por su nombre en una época que lo tildará de enjuiciador.

sa.prompt: 24. State the first purpose of discipline and how 2 Corinthians 2 completes the picture.
sa.model: The first purpose of all church discipline is the restoration of the sinner, not the punishment of sin. In 2 Corinthians 2 Paul shows restoration completed: the church is to forgive and comfort the now-repentant man and reaffirm their love to him, lest he be swallowed up with too much sorrow and lest Satan take advantage. Discipline that begins in love must end, where there is repentance, in glad reaffirmation. The goal throughout is to gain the brother.

es_reference.prompt: 24. Enuncie el primer propósito de la disciplina y cómo 2 Corintios 2 completa el cuadro.
es_reference.model: El primer propósito de toda disciplina de la iglesia es la restauración del pecador, no el castigo del pecado. En 2 Corintios 2 Pablo muestra la restauración consumada: la iglesia ha de perdonar y consolar al hombre ya arrepentido y confirmar su amor para con él, para que no sea consumido de demasiada tristeza y para que Satanás no gane ventaja. La disciplina que comienza en amor debe terminar, donde hay arrepentimiento, en gozosa confirmación. La meta en todo es ganar al hermano.

sa.prompt: 25. Distinguish godly sorrow from worldly sorrow and explain wise restoration.
sa.model: 2 Corinthians 7:10 distinguishes godly sorrow, which leads to repentance, from the sorrow of the world, which is mere regret at being caught. Wise restoration is therefore a process that is neither rushed nor refused. To restore a fallen leader too quickly, before repentance is tested, is a wound to the church and often to the man himself. Restoration often takes the form of a clear, written path with defined steps and a season of proven faithfulness.

es_reference.prompt: 25. Distinga la tristeza según Dios de la tristeza del mundo y explique la restauración sabia.
es_reference.model: 2 Corintios 7:10 distingue la tristeza según Dios, que lleva al arrepentimiento, de la tristeza del mundo, que es mero pesar por haber sido descubierto. Por eso la restauración sabia es un proceso que ni se apresura ni se rehúsa. Restaurar a un líder caído demasiado pronto, antes de probar el arrepentimiento, es una herida para la iglesia y a menudo para el hombre mismo. La restauración suele tomar la forma de un camino claro y escrito, con pasos definidos y una temporada de fidelidad probada.

sa.prompt: 26. Why does the unit insist Christian ethics is the fruit of a favor already given, not a ladder?
sa.model: The integrating truth of the whole course is that Christian ethics is never a ladder we climb to earn God's favor but the fruit of a favor already given. Everything taught has rested on grace first, then the holy life grace produces. The unit urges each minister to write his own Pastoral Ethics Statement, deciding in the calm what he will do in the storm. And echoing Unit 3 it reminds that no man falls all at once; he drifts, so vigilance must be deliberate.

es_reference.prompt: 26. ¿Por qué insiste la unidad en que la ética cristiana es el fruto de un favor ya dado, no una escalera?
es_reference.model: La verdad integradora de todo el curso es que la ética cristiana nunca es una escalera que subimos para ganar el favor de Dios, sino el fruto de un favor ya dado. Todo lo enseñado ha descansado en la gracia primero, y luego en la vida santa que la gracia produce. La unidad insta a cada ministro a escribir su propia Declaración de Ética Pastoral, decidiendo en la calma lo que hará en la tormenta. Y haciéndose eco de la Unidad 3 recuerda que ningún hombre cae de una vez; se desvía poco a poco, así que la vigilancia debe ser deliberada.

sa.prompt: 27. How does the great reversal of Luke 16 govern the way a pastor lives?
sa.model: In Luke 16 the rich man's sin toward Lazarus was that he stepped over him and did nothing; after death he lifted up his eyes and saw, too late, the beggar he had ignored now comforted. The great reversal ought to govern how a pastor lives because we will all one day lift up our eyes and give account. It presses the leader toward generosity and notice of the overlooked now, while there is time. How we treat the Lazarus at the gate is not a small matter but an eternal one.

es_reference.prompt: 27. ¿Cómo gobierna la gran inversión de Lucas 16 la manera en que vive un pastor?
es_reference.model: En Lucas 16 el pecado del rico hacia Lázaro fue que pasó por encima de él y no hizo nada; tras la muerte alzó sus ojos y vio, demasiado tarde, al mendigo que había ignorado ahora consolado. La gran inversión debe gobernar cómo vive un pastor, porque todos un día alzaremos nuestros ojos y daremos cuenta. Empuja al líder hacia la generosidad y a fijarse en el olvidado ahora, mientras hay tiempo. Cómo tratamos al Lázaro a la puerta no es asunto pequeño sino eterno.

sa.prompt: 28. How does the course mean to end, and what testimony frames a faithful finish?
sa.model: The course ends, as a faithful ministry ends, with the testimony first sounded in Unit 3: "I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith" (2 Timothy 4:7). The goal was never merely to begin well, nor to be admired, nor to avoid scandal. The goal is to finish: to stand at the last having been, by the grace of God, a faithful and holy shepherd of the flock He bought with His own blood. That is the capstone of the whole course, and it is reached by grace: the grace that called the minister keeps him to the end.

es_reference.prompt: 28. ¿Cómo pretende terminar el curso, y qué testimonio enmarca un final fiel?
es_reference.model: El curso termina, como termina un ministerio fiel, con el testimonio expresado por primera vez en la Unidad 3: "He peleado la buena batalla, he acabado la carrera, he guardado la fe" (2 Timoteo 4:7). La meta nunca fue solo comenzar bien, ni ser admirado, ni evitar el escándalo. La meta es terminar: estar de pie al final habiendo sido, por la gracia de Dios, un pastor fiel y santo del rebaño que Él compró con Su propia sangre. Ese es el remate de todo el curso, y se alcanza por gracia: la gracia que llamó al ministro lo guarda hasta el fin.

sa.prompt: 29. Why must obedience to the state sometimes yield, and what must the pastor teach his people about it?
sa.model: Obedience to governing authority is real, because the authorities are ordained of God (Romans 13:1) and Christians are to be subject to them, yet it is never absolute, for Caesar himself belongs to God. When the state commands what God forbids or forbids what God commands, the believer must obey God rather than men. The pastor must therefore teach his people to be the best of citizens and never the state's lapdogs, honoring the magistrate without ever handing him the conscience that belongs to God alone.

es_reference.prompt: 29. ¿Por qué debe ceder a veces la obediencia al Estado, y qué debe enseñar el pastor a su pueblo al respecto?
es_reference.model: La obediencia a la autoridad gobernante es real, porque las autoridades son ordenadas por Dios (Romanos 13:1) y los cristianos deben sujetarse a ellas, pero nunca es absoluta, pues el propio César pertenece a Dios. Cuando el Estado manda lo que Dios prohíbe o prohíbe lo que Dios manda, el creyente debe obedecer a Dios antes que a los hombres. El pastor debe, por tanto, enseñar a su pueblo a ser los mejores ciudadanos y nunca los siervos sumisos del Estado, honrando al magistrado sin entregarle jamás la conciencia que pertenece solo a Dios.

sa.prompt: 30. Tie together discernment, restoration, and the capstone as the unit's final word to the pastor.
sa.model: The unit gathers the course: judge with righteous, self-examined discernment rather than Pharisaism or cowardice; pursue the restoration of the fallen as discipline's first goal, neither rushing nor refusing it; and remember that ethics is the fruit of grace, not a ladder. Each minister should write his own Pastoral Ethics Statement and guard against the slow drift that ruins a ministry. We will all lift up our eyes and give account one day. So the final word is to finish faithfully—to keep the faith to the end.

es_reference.prompt: 30. Una el discernimiento, la restauración y la culminación como la palabra final de la unidad al pastor.
es_reference.model: La unidad reúne el curso: juzgar con discernimiento recto y examinado, no con fariseísmo ni cobardía; buscar la restauración del caído como primera meta de la disciplina, sin apresurarla ni rehusarla; y recordar que la ética es el fruto de la gracia, no una escalera. Cada ministro debe escribir su propia Declaración de Ética Pastoral y guardarse del lento desvío que arruina un ministerio. Todos alzaremos nuestros ojos y daremos cuenta un día. Así la última palabra es terminar fielmente, guardar la fe hasta el fin.
